title: Terumah: among them (Exodus 25:8)
hookLine: "that I may dwell among them", not in it; teachers read it as within each person

lines: THE HOUSE WAS NEVER THE POINT.
cards: People who build a house often say the same thing a year later: the house was never really the point. The point was the dinners, the kids' height marks on the doorframe, the friends on the couch at midnight.

The walls just made room for it. The Torah is about to spend chapter after chapter on a building: measurements in cubits, gold rings, wooden boards, curtains of blue and purple. Before any of that, one verse explains why.
And there's a tiny word in it, one Hebrew suffix, that readers have been unpacking for centuries.

teach.h: LET THEM MAKE ME A SANCTUARY.
teach.b: Here it is, in the old Jewish translation: "And let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them."
The Hebrew for dwell is shachan, the root of mishkan, the name for this portable sanctuary, the tabernacle, and of a later word, Shechinah, the indwelling presence of God. Now the tiny word.
The verse doesn't say that I may dwell in it, in the building.

It says b'tocham, among them, in their midst. Grammatically that's natural: God's presence will be in the middle of the camp. But many Jewish teachers, from the sixteenth century onward, read it more personally.
B'tocham can also mean within them. Make me a sanctuary, they read, and I will dwell within each one of them. The building is a means; the people are the dwelling.
Several commentators give this reading, and it became a favorite in Hasidic teaching. It doesn't erase the building: the Torah really does want the tabernacle built, in exact detail.

It just shows where the details are pointing. That idea mattered enormously later. When the Temple in Jerusalem was destroyed, Jews kept praying, studying and gathering, in homes, in synagogues, anywhere.
The sages called the synagogue a small sanctuary, borrowing a phrase from the prophet Ezekiel.
A presence that dwells among people can travel wherever people go.

how: Many Jewish teachers read Exodus 25:8 as saying God dwells within each person, and the synagogue has long been called a mikdash me'at, a small sanctuary; many Jews also set aside a quiet corner at home for prayer or study.

games.q: God asks for a sanctuary. you'd expect: that I may dwell in it. what does the verse actually say?
o: that I may dwell in it.
that I may dwell among them.
that I may visit once a year.
games.why: among them, b'tocham. many teachers read it: within each of them. the building points to the people.

practice: Look around for one small spot you could make quiet: a corner, a chair by a window, the car before you go in, or just this minute with your eyes closed. No gold or blue curtains needed, only a little space set apart.
Sit in it now, and if you pray, invite the presence the verse speaks of; if not, notice what it's like to be still, here, inside yourself.
